brief: A tool caddy with a carry handle and divided bins for screws and bits.

requirements.evidence: Three cells in a row (piece -1,0 / 0,0 / 1,0), capped on the open sides and bolted together with 2 joint bolts. The configurator checks fit only: it doesn't check strength or load when carried.
handle:0,0,0;top on cover:0,0,0;full;top over the middle cell, so it sits at the centre of the caddy.

requirements.requirement: Divided bins for screws and bits
requirements.evidence: bin:-1,0,0 and bin:1,0,0 are each hex-bin-full-div3, giving 6 compartments. Screws, nuts and standoffs are shown in them. There's no driver-bit prop, so no bits are shown, but the compartments suit small bits.

finish.summary: I built a 3-cell tool caddy in a row. The middle cell has a top cover with a carry handle on it. Each end cell has a full-depth bin with 3 compartments, so there are 6 divided compartments in all. capOpenFaces put solid caps on every open side face, and lockJoints bolted the two joints between cells. The build has 30 parts and is estimated at about 1651 g of filament and 2343 minutes of printing. check_build passed with no issues and the mesh-collision check reads clear. For display, the left bin holds piles of screws, nuts and standoffs, and the right bin holds screws, a pen and a marker. The prop catalogue has no driver bits, and a 2 mm hex driver wouldn't fit standing in a compartment. Those props aren't part of the build. The piles of screws sit below the bin rims, so you can only see them from above. That's normal for a caddy.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
